questions.q: What is moral courage, as the summary defines it?
a: Acting on your principles even at personal risk
Facing physical danger on a battlefield
Ignoring criticism from people you respect
Speaking only when you are sure of winning
questions.why: Lesson 1 separates moral courage, which follows your moral compass, from physical courage in the face of danger.

questions.q: Which example of moral courage does the summary give?
a: A whistleblower who reports wrongdoing despite the risk
A soldier charging into enemy fire
A firefighter entering a burning building
An athlete competing through an injury
questions.why: The summary names the whistleblower as someone who acts on principle knowing it may put them at risk.

questions.q: How does Holiday suggest overcoming fear?
a: Analyze it logically and define its real size
Avoid the situation until the fear fades
Repeat affirmations until you feel brave
Wait for someone else to act first
questions.why: Lesson 2 says fear grows when it stays vague, so reason and clear definition shrink it to its true size.

a: Anticipating a fear before it happens
Listing everything you are grateful for
Imagining the worst and then giving up
Practicing public speaking in private
questions.why: The summary describes fear setting as preparing for feared outcomes in advance so they can hurt you less.

questions.q: How does the author say courage is built?
a: Through small, repeated acts of bravery
By waiting for one great moment to act
By reading stories about heroic people
By removing all risk from your life
questions.why: Lesson 3 compares courage to any skill and advises starting small rather than waiting for a grand gesture.
